content: Intrinsic factor (IF), also referred to as gastric intrinsic factor (GIF), is a glycoprotein synthesized by the parietal cells of the stomach. It plays a critical role in the absorption of vitamin B12, which occurs later in the ileum of the small intestine. Haptocorrin, also known as HC, R protein, or transcobalamin I (TCN1), is another glycoprotein secreted by the salivary glands. It binds to vitamin B12, protecting it from the acidic environment of the stomach. Vitamin B12 is acid-sensitive, and its binding to transcobalamin I allows it to safely traverse the stomach and reach the duodenum. In the less acidic environment of the small intestine, pancreatic enzymes degrade the glycoprotein carrier, allowing vitamin B12 to bind to intrinsic factor. This newly formed complex is then absorbed by the epithelial cells (enterocytes) of the ileum. Within these cells, vitamin B12 dissociates from intrinsic factor and binds to another protein, transcobalamin II (TCN2). This new complex exits the epithelial cells and is transported to the liver for storage and further use. Intrinsic factor is secreted by the stomach and is present in both gastric juice and the gastric mucosal membrane. Its optimal pH for activity is approximately 7. Intrinsic factor can still be present even in the absence of significant pepsin activity. The site of intrinsic factor production varies among species. In humans, it is produced in the fundus and body of the stomach, while in pigs, it is secreted from the pylorus and the beginning of the duodenum. The limited production of intrinsic factor in humans restricts the efficient absorption of vitamin B12 to about 2 micrograms per meal, which is generally sufficient for normal dietary intake. In pernicious anemia, an autoimmune condition, autoantibodies targeting intrinsic factor or the parietal cells themselves result in intrinsic factor deficiency. This leads to impaired absorption of vitamin B12 and subsequent megaloblastic anemia. Atrophic gastritis can also cause intrinsic factor deficiency and anemia by damaging the parietal cells of the stomach lining. Additionally, pancreatic exocrine insufficiency can interfere with the normal dissociation of vitamin B12 from its binding proteins in the small intestine, preventing its absorption via the intrinsic factor complex. Other risk factors for pernicious anemia include conditions that damage or remove portions of the stomach's parietal cells, such as bariatric surgery, gastric tumors, gastric ulcers, and excessive alcohol consumption. Rarely, mutations in the GIF gene can cause an inheritable form of intrinsic factor deficiency, resulting in malabsorption of vitamin B12. Treatment for pernicious anemia typically involves intramuscular injections of vitamin B12 in most countries. Oral administration of vitamin B12 is also effective, even in the absence of intrinsic factor, though the absorption rate is less than 1% compared to when intrinsic factor is present. Despite the low absorption rate, oral vitamin B12 therapy has been shown to effectively alleviate symptoms of pernicious anemia. Sublingual administration of vitamin B12 is another option, but there is no evidence to suggest it is superior to oral administration. Although oral vitamin B12 treatment is effective, only Canada and Sweden routinely prescribe this method of administration.
